title: Judicial Renaissance -- Ch. 11: Liberty and Prosperity
keywords: Alleviating Poverty and Resolving the Fiscal Crisis
The World Bank in a Changing World
Department of Agrarian Reform v. Cuenca
Sta. Rosa Realty Development Corporation v. Amante
La Bugal-B'laan Tribal Association v. Ramos
primary_topics: Chapter 11 of 'Judicial Renaissance' -- the speech CJP delivered before the IBP's 10th National Convention of Lawyers in Baguio City, arguing that the rule of law must safeguard not only liberty but also prosperity, and that the legal profession has a concrete, active role in alleviating poverty and easing the fiscal crisis.

The convergence of development economics and judicial reform: the World Bank's and the Asian Development Bank's finding that without effective laws and structures there can be no investment and no growth, and the ADB's redefinition of poverty as a deprivation of essential assets and opportunities.

The Supreme Court's role in economic development: a general rule of deference to the political branches on economic policy, with intervention only where an act is executed with grave abuse of discretion, illustrated by Tanada v. Angara and by the La Bugal-B'laan mining ruling and its favorable market aftermath.

A six-part program of action for the bar: proactive initiation of cases promoting development, legal accountability and transparency in public funds, the fight against corruption within and outside the profession, legal empowerment of the poor, institutional mechanisms for social sharing, and personal lives of rectitude.
sub_topics: CJP opens by thanking Atty. Angelica Y. Santiago and IBP president Atty. Jose Anselmo I. Cadiz for the invitation to the 10th National Convention of Lawyers in Baguio City.

He praises Cadiz's inaugural speech and his 'psychedelic choice of heroes' -- the Kennedys, Ho Chi Minh, Nelson Mandela and Jose Abad Santos -- judged by his high school teacher's maxim about friends revealing character.
He recalls Justice J. B. L. Reyes's mid-70s lament that some attorneys acted as 'hired guns' for moneyed clients, and reads the convention theme as the bar's repudiation of that professional morass.
The conference theme is aligned with the Catholic Church's Eucharistic Prayer describing a people wounded by political conflict, unjust socio-economic divisions and corruption.
Law maintains social order and courts are 'the great arbiters of all time,' but interest in law's impact on poverty has opened a new dimension of the justice system's utility.
He quotes Dr. Ibrahim F. I. Shihata's 1995 World Bank report and describes the ADB's law and policy reform activities and its new asset-and-opportunity definition of poverty.
He insists the 1987 Constitution itself suffices as authority: its directives on social justice, human rights, ecology, women, children, labor and indigenous cultural communities.
He cites the Court's pro-poor rulings in agrarian reform, human rights, labor, environment and economic development, singling out DAR v. Cuenca and Sta. Rosa Realty v. Amante.
Drawing on his book Leveling the Playing Field, he describes how markets react to major Court rulings and states the laissez-faire doctrine of deference absent grave abuse of discretion.
He quotes Tanada v. Angara on the great respect owed the Senate as a coordinate constitutional body whose acts are presumed regular.

He reports the La Bugal-B'laan Decision on RA 7942 as the longest in the Court's 104-year history at 246 pages, and credits its December 1, 2004 issuance with a 'sunshine effect' on investments, the stock market, the peso and the IPOs of Manila Water and SM Investments.
First task for the bar: because the judiciary is a passive actor, lawyers must proactively initiate, prosecute or defend cases and causes that promote economic development.
Second: ensure legal accountability and transparency in the use of public funds, beginning with educational and information campaigns stressing accountability for every peso.

Third: shun and report corruption, including corruption by lawyers who fold bribe money into attorney's fees, and consider the SWS-surveyed proposals -- prosecuting corrupt lawyers and officials, protecting whistleblowers, lifestyle checks, and client termination agreements.
Fourth: push legal empowerment per an ADB-commissioned study -- raising legal awareness, extending legal assistance, and ensuring the poor participate in local governance structures.

Fifth: build mechanisms for 'social sharing,' invoking Jeffrey D. Sachs's The End of Poverty and the Ateneo's '10-Point Agenda for Economic Democratization,' with the arithmetic that if one of every three non-poor families nurtures one poor family, poverty ends.

Sixth and most personal: lawyers should lead lives of rectitude -- paying correct taxes on time, observing rules, living modestly and giving everyone their just share under the Civil Code's human relations provisions.
He closes by commending the IBP's choice of theme while challenging it to expand its horizon toward the twin goals of safeguarding liberty and nurturing prosperity.

stances.claim: The rule of law must secure not only liberty but prosperity: there can be no meaningful economic development without an effective rule of law in place, which is why development agencies now fund judicial and legal reform as a prerequisite to poverty reduction.
stances.rhetorical_move: argument from external authority -- stacking the Catholic Church, the World Bank, the ADB and then the 1987 Constitution, while noting that the Charter alone would have sufficed

stances.claim: As a general rule the Supreme Court defers to the agencies with primary responsibility for economic development and intervenes only when an act is clearly made or executed with grave abuse of discretion.
stances.rhetorical_move: rule-and-exception framing, anchored in the Tanada v. Angara presumption of regularity owed a coordinate constitutional body

stances.claim: The bar itself must shun corruption by reporting it, because corruption in the judiciary persists only where lawyers tolerate or abet it -- and lawyers who fold bribe money into their fees are worse offenders than the judges they complain about.
stances.rhetorical_move: turning the complaint back on the complainants, backed by SWS survey findings and a concrete menu of remedial actions

stances.claim: Poverty can be ended through 'social sharing' if one of every three non-poor Filipino families helps nurture one poor family out of poverty, an idea the legal profession can give institutional form.
stances.rhetorical_move: arithmetic illustration plus the provocative analogy to community adoption of endangered species

notable_anecdotes: CJP recalls Atty. Cadiz's inaugural speech at the Supreme Court Session Hall two years earlier and his 'psychedelic choice of heroes' -- the Kennedys, Ho Chi Minh, Mandela and Abad Santos -- rating him a perfect 10 by his high school teacher's maxim, 'Tell me who your friends are and I will tell you who you are.'
He recounts Justice J. B. L. Reyes's constant reminder to new lawyers in the mid-70s that law is a means to serve justice, and his lament about attorneys behaving as 'hired guns.'

He reports the market aftermath of the December 1, 2004 mining Decision -- rising foreign investment, a revived stock market, a better peso rate, and the oversubscribed IPOs of Manila Water and SM Investments -- as the 'sunshine effect' that spread beyond the mining sector.

He points to the Philippine practice of entrusting crocodiles, tarsiers, eagles and other endangered species to the care of communities and families, and asks whether people could not be adopted the same way.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 11 of 'Judicial Renaissance' reproduces the address Justice Panganiban delivered to the Integrated Bar of the Philippines' 10th National Convention of Lawyers in Baguio City, hosted by Atty. Angelica Y. Santiago and IBP president Atty. Jose Anselmo I. Cadiz, whose inaugural speech and 'psychedelic choice of heroes' -- the Kennedys, Ho Chi Minh, Nelson Mandela and Jose Abad Santos -- he praised by his old teacher's maxim that one is known by one's friends. Recalling Justice J. B. L. Reyes's lament that some attorneys behaved as 'hired guns' for their moneyed clients, he read the convention theme, 'Alleviating Poverty and Resolving the Fiscal Crisis,' as the profession's pledge to free the people not only from fear but from want, and aligned it with the Church's Eucharistic Prayer for a wounded people. He argued that law maintains social order and that development agencies now treat legal and judicial reform as a prerequisite to growth, quoting Dr. Ibrahim F. I. Shihata's 1995 World Bank report and describing the Asian Development Bank's law and policy reform work and its redefinition of poverty as a deprivation of assets and opportunities; the 1987 Constitution, he added, already supplied ample authority through its directives on social justice, human rights, ecology, labor and indigenous communities, as the Court's rulings in Department of Agrarian Reform v. Cuenca and Sta. Rosa Realty v. Amante showed. Drawing on his book Leveling the Playing Field, he set out the Court's laissez-faire posture -- deference to the economic agencies except where grave abuse of discretion appears, as Tanada v. Angara illustrates -- and reported that the 246-page La Bugal-B'laan Decision, the longest in the Court's 104-year history, had produced a 'sunshine effect' on investment, the stock market, the peso and the Manila Water and SM Investments offerings. He then charged the bar with six tasks: initiating development-promoting cases, enforcing accountability and transparency in public funds, reporting and refusing corruption, pursuing legal empowerment of the poor along ADB-recommended lines, building mechanisms for 'social sharing' after Jeffrey D. Sachs and the Ateneo's 10-Point Agenda, and leading lives of rectitude. He closed by commending the IBP's theme and urging concrete measures toward the twin goals of safeguarding liberty and nurturing prosperity.
